title: Library
summary: The papers, books and blog posts the author reads, in the app.
description: What the book draws on sits next to it: papers, books and blog posts, each a PDF, a text or both, with a few details, readable on every device.

stories.as: an author who reads papers and books to write about them
stories.want: my papers and books in the same app as the book
stories.soThat: what I read is at hand on every device where I write

stories.as: an author adding papers in bulk
stories.want: their details filled in for me
stories.soThat: I never type in a title or an author list

stories.as: an author working through a long book
stories.want: its table of contents beside it
stories.soThat: I can go straight to the chapter I need

stories.as: an author reading a paper on my phone
stories.want: the page to fill the screen and zoom like any reader app
stories.soThat: reading on the phone is as easy as on paper

stories.as: an author following new papers on arXiv
stories.want: to add a paper by its arXiv number
stories.soThat: I don't download and upload files by hand

stories.as: an author reading papers on my phone
stories.want: papers as text that fits the screen
stories.soThat: reading on the phone is as easy as on a computer

stories.as: an author who comes across things to read on my phone
stories.want: to share a post or a PDF to the app from wherever I found it
stories.soThat: it's in the library without copying addresses or downloading files

stories.as: an author who follows discussions on Hacker News
stories.want: to keep a whole thread in the library, by its address or by sharing it to the app, and see it grow
stories.soThat: I can read it offline, come back to what's new, and still read what was said after it's edited or deleted

requirements.text: The library holds papers, books and blog posts, each with a PDF, an HTML version, or both, and discussion threads, each with its comments.

history.text: The library holds papers and books, each with one PDF file.
history.reason: The author reads blog posts as well as papers and books, and wants them in the library beside them. A post has no PDF: its text is its HTML version, as an HTML file's is.

history.text: The library holds papers, books and blog posts, each with a PDF, an HTML version, or both.
history.reason: The author keeps discussions from Hacker News beside what they discuss, to read offline and come back to as they grow. A thread is neither a PDF nor a page: it's a story and its comments.

requirements.text: The author adds an item to the library by uploading a PDF of at most `library.max-file-size`.
Each item has a title, authors, a year and a kind from `library.kinds`.
When an item is added, a model reads its first pages and fills in its title, authors, the authors' institutions, its year and its kind.

history.text: When an item is added, its title, authors and year are taken from the PDF's own metadata where the PDF has them.
history.reason: The author won't type details in, and a PDF's own metadata is often missing or wrong.

requirements.text: The author can edit an item's details.
An item's PDF can be read in the app on every platform in `app.platforms`.
An item's PDF is stored in the database and syncs to the book's devices with the rest of the book.
The author can remove an item, and its PDF with it, from the library.
Where no model can be asked (no key, no network), an item's details are taken from the PDF's own metadata.
Details are read with `library.details-model` unless the author chose another model.
The model reads an item's details when it is added, and again only when the author asks.
Only the text of an item's first `library.details-pages` pages goes to the model, or images of them when the PDF has no text.
Text in a PDF can be selected and copied in the viewer.
An item's table of contents is taken from the PDF's own outline, with the page each entry starts on, where the PDF has one.
The viewer shows an item's table of contents, marks the entry being read, and goes to an entry's page when it is chosen.
An item added before tables of contents were taken gets one the first time its PDF is opened.
A PDF shows its first page without waiting for its other pages to be measured.

Pages zoom with a pinch, keeping the point between the fingers in place, and a double tap switches between fitting the width and `pdf.double-tap-zoom` times that; on a computer, Ctrl or ⌘ with the scroll wheel zooms.

On a phone, everything around what's read (the item's bar and authors, the viewer's controls, the app's buttons over it) steps aside while scrolling down through a PDF or text, and comes back on scrolling up, or on tapping a PDF's page.

history.text: On a phone, the viewer's controls and the app's buttons over it hide while scrolling down through a PDF, and come back on scrolling up or tapping the page.
history.reason: Read as text, a long author list and the bars took the phone's screen from the paper; text reads with the same room as a PDF.

requirements.text: An item opened at an address that names no page reopens at the page last read on that device.

history.text: The viewer reopens an item at the page last read on that device.
history.reason: The item's address now names the page in view (LIB-22); a page in the address comes first, so a link to a page goes there.

requirements.text: The author can go to a page of a PDF by its number.
An item's address holds the PDF page in view, `#page=<n>`, so a link can open a PDF at a page.

The author can add a paper from arXiv by its identifier, such as `1706.03762`, or its address. Its title, authors and year come from arXiv's listing, and its PDF and, where arXiv has one, its HTML version come with it.
An item can hold an HTML version, from arXiv or from an HTML file the author adds; like a PDF, it syncs.

An item with an HTML version can be read as text that fits the screen, with its sections as its contents and its maths shown as maths. On a phone it opens as text, on a computer as its PDF where it has one; the author can switch.
Read as text, an item's address holds that it's read as text and the section at the top of the view.
An HTML version keeps its figures, so it reads the same offline.

The author adds a blog post by its address. Its text and figures, as the page shows them once it has run (a page that builds itself in the browser included), without the site's navigation and the like, become the item's HTML version; its title, authors and date come from the page where it gives them, and the model reads the rest. Only the address leaves the device. Adding an address already in the library opens it.
An address the author adds that serves a PDF adds that PDF, as adding the file would; so does the address of a page that only shows a PDF file, as a code host shows a file it holds.

history.text: An address the author adds that serves a PDF adds that PDF, as adding the file would.
history.reason: A paper shared from GitHub is the address of GitHub's page for the file, which shows the PDF in a viewer of its own; read as a post, it added the page's frame instead of the paper.

requirements.text: On a phone, the author can share to the app from any other app: a web address, or one or more PDFs. Each is added to the library as if the author had added it there (an address by the Hacker News thread's address in what's shared, else its first web address or arXiv number), the library shows it being added, and a single item opens once it's in.

history.text: On a phone, the author can share to the app from any other app: a web address, or one or more PDFs. Each is added to the library as if the author had added it there (an address by the first web address or arXiv number in what's shared), the library shows it being added, and a single item opens once it's in.
history.reason: What's shared from Hacker News can carry the article's address beside the thread's; the author shares the discussion, so the thread's address wins.

requirements.text: The author adds a Hacker News thread by its address, in the library or by sharing it to the app: the story and every comment in it, kept on the device so it reads offline. The address of one of its comments adds the whole thread and opens it at that comment. Adding a thread already in the library opens it.

A thread reads as the site shows it: the story, with a link to what it's about and its own text, then its comments nested under what they answer, in the site's order, each with its author and when it was written. A comment's replies can be folded away.

A thread looks for new, edited and deleted comments each time it's opened while the device is online, and when the author asks; it says when it last did. Comments that arrived since the author last opened it on this device are marked as new.
A comment deleted or removed on the site stays in the thread as it was last seen, marked as gone from the site. One deleted before the thread was kept shows as a placeholder where it has replies.
A comment, or the story's text, edited on the site shows its latest text, marked as edited, and keeps every earlier text the library saw, which the author can read beside it.
